title: Modern Java Enhancements
intro: The language features added since Java 5: generics, collections and the enhanced for loop, lambdas and streams, default methods, and the enhanced switch. Expect questions that ask you to read short code and predict the output.

cards.title: Why generics? Compile-time type safety
cards.body:
Before Java 5 a `List` held plain `Object`s. You could add anything, and you had to cast when reading. A wrong cast compiled fine and crashed at **run time** with a ClassCastException.

With generics, `List<String>` tells the compiler the element type. `add(2)` is rejected at **compile time**, and `get()` returns a String with no cast.

cards.title: Generic classes, type parameters and <>
cards.body:
A generic class declares **type parameters** in angle brackets: `class Box<T>`. `T` is a placeholder; you supply a real type when you use the class: `Box<Integer>`. A class may have several: `Box<T, U>`.

The **diamond operator** `<>` (Java 7) lets the compiler infer the type arguments on the right side: `List<String> list = new ArrayList<>();` instead of repeating `ArrayList<String>`.

cards.title: Generic methods, bounded types and erasure
cards.body:
A **generic method** declares its own type parameter before the return type: `static <T> T first(List<T> list)`. The compiler infers T from the arguments.

A **bounded type** `<T extends Number>` limits T to Number or its subclasses. In exchange you may call Number's methods (like `doubleValue()`) on a T.
cards.after: **Type erasure:** generics exist only at compile time. The compiler checks the types, then erases T to Object (or to its bound). At run time a `List<String>` and a `List<Integer>` are the same class, so you cannot write `new T()` or `x instanceof List<String>`.
keypoints: `<T>` before the return type = generic method.
`<T extends X>` = upper bound; T can use X's methods.
Erasure: type info is checked, then removed; it is not there at run time.

cards.title: Wildcards: ? extends, ? super, ?
cards.body:
A wildcard `?` stands for "some unknown type" in a parameter.

`List<? extends Fruit>` (**upper bounded**) accepts a list of Fruit, Apple or Banana. You can **read** elements as Fruit, but can't add (the real list might be List<Banana>).
`List<? super Fruit>` (**lower bounded**) accepts a list of Fruit, Food or Object. You can **add** a Fruit or Apple, but reading gives only Object.
`List<?>` (**unbounded**) accepts any list; read elements as Object.

cards.title: The Collections Framework hierarchy
cards.body:
Collections are generic containers in `java.util`. **Iterable → Collection** is the root of List, Queue and Set. **Map** is a separate hierarchy: it stores key→value pairs and is **not** a Collection.

Interfaces (green) say what you can do; classes (orange) are implementations. Declare variables with the interface type: `List<String> l = new ArrayList<>();`

cards.title: Lambda expressions and functional interfaces
cards.body:
A lambda (Java 8) is a short way to write an anonymous function: `(arguments) -> { body }`. It replaces a bulky anonymous class.

A lambda needs a target type that is a **functional interface**: an interface with **exactly one abstract method** (can be marked `@FunctionalInterface`, like Runnable). The lambda becomes that method's body.

cards.title: Streams: source → intermediate → terminal
cards.body: The Streams API (Java 8) processes data in a pipeline. A **source** (collection, array) creates a stream. **Intermediate** operations such as `filter`, `map` and `sorted` each return a new stream. A **terminal** operation such as `collect`, `forEach`, `reduce` or `count` produces the result.

cards.title: Default methods in interfaces
cards.body:
A **default method** is an interface method with a body, marked `default` (Java 8). Why: to **evolve an API**. Adding a new abstract method to an interface would break every existing implementer; adding a default method doesn't.

Interfaces can also have **static** methods: helpers called as `Printer.info()`. They are not inherited and can't be overridden.

cards.title: Enhanced switch (Java 12+)
cards.body:
The arrow form `case X -> ...` runs **only** the matching case: **no fall-through**, no `break`. One case can list **several labels**: `case 'A', 'B' ->`.

A switch can be an **expression** that returns a value: `int n = switch (x) { ... };` (note the final `;`). When a case needs a block, `yield` gives the block's value.

keypoints: Mistake: `List<int>`. Type arguments must be classes: `List<Integer>`.
Mistake: thinking a stream runs without a terminal operation. It is lazy.
Mistake: `x, y -> x + y`. Two or more parameters need brackets: `(x, y) -> x + y`.
Mistake: forgetting that Map is not a Collection, and that `put` on an existing key replaces the value.
Mistake: expecting fall-through with `->`. Only the matching case runs.
